questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Integral of a Logarithmic Expression Using Integration by Parts Twice
questions.worked_solution:
We need to use integration by parts.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u={ln}^{2}⁡(x)\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{ln}^{2}⁡x}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({ln}^{2}⁡(x))(-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}})-\int (-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}})(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡(x)}{2{x}^{2}}+\int \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\int \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{{x}^{3}}\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x))(-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}})-\int (-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}})(\frac{1}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{2{x}^{2}}+\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{2{x}^{2}}-\frac{1}{4{x}^{2}}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an integral constant.

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{ln}^{2}⁡x}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡(x)}{2{x}^{2}}+(-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{2{x}^{2}}-\frac{1}{4{x}^{2}}+C) \\  & =-\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡(x)}{2{x}^{2}}-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{2{x}^{2}}-\frac{1}{4{x}^{2}}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{4{x}^{2}}(2{ln}^{2}⁡(x)+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+1)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Integral of a Trigonometric Expression Using Integration by Parts Twice
questions.worked_solution:
We need to use integration by parts. 

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=5{x}^{2}+1\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=10x \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 5{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(5{x}^{2}+1)(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(10x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-(5{x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+10\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we use integration by parts to evaluate  $\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1 \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(x)(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant.

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (5{x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =-(5{x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+10(x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x+D) \\  & =-(5{x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+10x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+10\operatorname{cos}⁡x+10D \\  & =(9-5{x}^{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡x+10x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=10D.$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Integral of a Logarithmic Expression Using Integration by Parts Twice
questions.worked_solution:
We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \,\text{d}x=x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}(x)-\int (x)(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =x{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-2\int \operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\int \operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \,\text{d}x=x.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x))(x)-\int (x)(\frac{1}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)-\int \text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)-x+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is a constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =x{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-2(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)-x+D) \\  & =x{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+2x+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-2D.$ 

Finally then, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & ={(x{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+2x)|}_{1}^{e} \\  & =(e{(\operatorname{ln}⁡e)}^{2}-2e\operatorname{ln}⁡(e)+2e)-(1{(\operatorname{ln}⁡1)}^{2}-2\cdot 1\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)+2(1)) \\  & =e-2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Integral of a Trigonometric Expression Using Integration by Parts Twice
questions.worked_solution:
We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=4{x}^{2}+3\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=8x \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula for integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (4{x}^{2}+3)\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(4{x}^{2}+3)(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(8x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-(4{x}^{2}+3)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+8\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we use integration by parts to evaluate $\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x & \,⟹\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,dx \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (4{x}^{2}+3)\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =-(4{x}^{2}+3)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+8\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-(4{x}^{2}+3)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+8(x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x+D) \\  & =-(4{x}^{2}+3)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+8x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+8\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=8D.$

Finally, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(4{x}^{2}+3)\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={[-(4{x}^{2}+3)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+8x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+8\operatorname{cos}⁡x]}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =(-(4{\pi }^{2}+3)\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi +8\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi +8\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi )-(-3\operatorname{cos}⁡0+8(0)\operatorname{sin}⁡0+8\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =(4{\pi }^{2}+3-8)-(-3+8) \\  & =4{\pi }^{2}-5-5 \\  & =4{\pi }^{2}-10\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))^{2} & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=12{x}^{2} & \,⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int 12{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=4{x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 12{x}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))}^{2}(4{x}^{3})-\int (4{x}^{3})(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))}^{2}-8\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x) & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={x}^{2} & \,⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})-\int (\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})(\frac{1}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)}{3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{9}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 12{x}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))^{2}\,\text{d}x & =4{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))}^{2}-8\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))}^{2}-8(\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)}{3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{9}+D) \\  & =4{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))}^{2}-\frac{8{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)}{3}+\frac{8{x}^{3}}{9}-8D \\  & ={x}^{3}(4{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))}^{2}-\frac{8}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)+\frac{8}{9})+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-8D.$

Finally, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1/2}^{e/2}12{x}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))^{2}\text{d}x & ={[{x}^{3}(4{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))}^{2}-\frac{8}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)+\frac{8}{9})]}_{1/2}^{e/2} \\  & =[{(\frac{e}{2})}^{3}(4{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot \frac{e}{2}))}^{2}-\frac{8}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot \frac{e}{2})+\frac{8}{9})] \\  & \,-[{(\frac{1}{2})}^{3}(4{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot \frac{1}{2}))}^{2}-\frac{8}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot \frac{1}{2})+\frac{8}{9})] \\  & =[\frac{{e}^{3}}{8}(4{(\operatorname{ln}⁡e)}^{2}-\frac{8}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡e+\frac{8}{9})]-[\frac{1}{8}(4{(\operatorname{ln}⁡1)}^{2}-\frac{8}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡1+\frac{8}{9})] \\  & =[\frac{{e}^{3}}{8}(4-\frac{8}{3}+\frac{8}{9})]-\frac{1}{8}\cdot \frac{8}{9} \\  & =\frac{5{e}^{3}-2}{18}\end{aligned}
$$
